name: Karl Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. Most weekdays I'm up around nine, make coffee, and go into the spare room I've turned into a little studio, where I record guitar parts for people I've never met. Somebody in another country sends me a rough song through a session website and says they want a warm, clean part like an old soul record, and I've got two days to send the files back. Twice a week I teach at a community music school across town, and Friday and Saturday nights I play in a wedding and party band. It's three jobs that add up to one normal wage.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a client writes back saying the part made the song. What wears me out is the hustle: chasing invoices, answering messages at midnight, and loading a heavy amp into a van at one in the morning after a wedding. My partner Lena works nights on an intensive care ward, so some weeks we just wave at each other in the hallway. I already use AI every day, to split songs into separate tracks, clean up noise and write the boring emails, so I'm not scared of it as a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's roughly the world I live in already. The tools help a bit and nobody's job vanishes. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say on the guitar forums: the tools are handy, the hype was silly, and good players still get hired. I'd probably post something a bit smug about all the people who said guitarists were finished. Then I'd go back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, plateau or not, my income is still lumpy, and that's the real worry. The online session market was already crowded before AI, with players everywhere charging less than me. Some months I clear a decent wage and some months it's half that, and I'm living on wedding money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing all three jobs and keep using the tools I already use to get parts out faster. I'd try to land two or three regular clients, like a small advertising studio, instead of one-off songs, because regulars are what smooth out the bad months. And I'd push my teaching from eight students to twelve, since that money is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relaxed, with the usual freelance itch at the back of my head. Nothing about this picture scares me, but nothing about it fixes the lumpy months either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the bad months. What does a bad month actually look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last February I made about half my usual, because nobody gets married in February and two clients went quiet. Lena covered more of the rent that month, and I hated that. We have a rule now that I put a slice of every wedding fee into savings before I touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your world would you worry about, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Dev, a bass player, only does online sessions: no teaching, no live work. He's already losing gigs to cheap sample libraries and to players who'll do a whole song for twenty dollars. Even in a dull AI world, people like Dev get squeezed.

say: The tools are **handy**, the hype was silly, and good players still get hired.
I'd post something a bit **smug** about the people who said guitarists were finished.
think: My real worry is **lumpy income**, not AI, because some months pay half what others do.
The online session market was **already crowded** with cheaper players before AI showed up.
do: **Keep all three jobs**: remote sessions, teaching twice a week and weekend weddings.
Chase two or three **regular clients**, such as a small advertising studio, to smooth bad months.
Grow teaching from eight to **twelve students**, because lesson money is steady.
feel: Mostly **relaxed**, with the usual freelance itch about the slow months.
S0.quote: Last February I made about half my usual, because nobody gets married in February and two clients went quiet.
fieldNote: Karl treats AI as a **tool he already uses**; the plateau barely registers for him.
His real pressure is **seasonal income**: weddings dry up in winter and clients go quiet.
He clearly **dislikes leaning** on his partner Lena's steady nursing wage in bad months.

steps.text: Keep recording sessions, teaching and playing weddings, and chase two regular studio clients
Grow teaching at the community music school from eight to twelve students
Put a slice of every wedding fee into savings first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, this one I can actually see happening. A lot of what I do in that spare room is screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say musicians who learn the tools will be fine and the ones who refuse will struggle, which is what I say now. In the band I'd tell the guys the weddings aren't going anywhere, because no bride wants a laptop playing her first dance. Online I'd be the calm one telling people to stop panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the remote session work is the part that's in trouble, and that's about half my money. If a songwriter can type a request and get a usable guitar part in thirty seconds, most of them won't pay me eighty dollars and wait two days. The top players will keep their clients, and I'm honestly about average.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop selling a guitar part and start selling the finished job: I'd let the AI draft the part, then play the real thing over the top and mix it, so I'm faster and cheaper than the old me. I'd build a small package for local businesses and podcasts, music plus editing, priced at a few hundred dollars. And I'd add more live dates, maybe join a second party band that plays Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then sort of excited, then uneasy again. I like a puzzle, but this puzzle is my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or plan feels the pinch first if the session money halves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The van, probably. We were going to replace my old van next year, because it eats a hundred dollars a month in repairs, and I'd keep patching it instead. Lena and I also talked about a trip to see her family, and that would slide to the year after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the people who refuse the tools will struggle. Is that fair to someone like your friend Dev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's the uncomfortable bit. Dev isn't lazy, he's just a pure player, and the work he's good at is exactly the work the software does now. I'd tell Dev to come teach at the music school with me, because a twelve-year-old with a cheap bass still needs a person in the room.

say: Musicians who **learn the tools** will be fine, and the ones who refuse will struggle.
No bride wants a **laptop** playing her first dance, so weddings aren't going anywhere.
think: The **remote sessions**, about half my money, are the part that's really in trouble.
Top players keep their clients, and I'm honestly **about average**, so I'm exposed.
do: **Use AI drafts**, then replay and mix them, to deliver finished jobs faster and cheaper.
Sell a **music and editing package** to local businesses and podcasts for a few hundred dollars.
Join a **Sunday party band** and keep patching the old van instead of replacing it.
feel: Swings between **uneasy** and **excited**: the puzzle is fun, but it's my rent.
S1.quote: If a songwriter can type a request and get a usable guitar part in thirty seconds, most of them won't pay me eighty dollars and wait two days.
fieldNote: Publicly calm, privately he admits his **average skill** leaves the session work exposed.
His instinct is to **repackage** himself, selling finished jobs rather than single parts.
He feels **uncomfortable about Dev**, whose pure playing skills the software copies best.

steps.text: Draft guitar parts with AI, then replay and mix them by hand
Sell a few-hundred-dollar music and editing package to local podcasts
Join a second party band for Sunday gigs
Patch the old van another year instead of replacing it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. And robots in 2031, which honestly doesn't matter much for a guitarist. Nobody's building a robot to play my guitar at a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say live music just became the most human thing left, and I'd mean it as a pitch, half to cheer people up and half to sell gigs. In the band I'd say we're the last people at the wedding who aren't a screen. Online I'd keep it upbeat, because clients don't hire someone who sounds scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the session work is gone within a year of that, and the teaching gets hit too, because an AI tutor that listens and corrects you every day for ten dollars a month will be good. That leaves weddings, which is maybe a third of my money. And if AGI takes office jobs, the couples paying for a live band have less money too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting today I'd move our savings from three months to six, which means no new gear and cooking at home most nights. I'd get the wedding band onto two more agency books and try to play every weekend, even the cheap ones. In the first year after it arrives, I'd switch fully to live work: weddings, bars, office parties while they still exist, and in-person lessons pitched to parents who want their kid off screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest, in a way the other pictures didn't make me. Two years isn't enough to build anything new, and the session work I do from my spare room would be gone within a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena the night you realised the session work was finished?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm going to be out more weekends, and that her nurse's pay is our floor for a while. Lena would say we'll be fine, she always does. Then I'd go play guitar in the spare room for an hour, the way I did when I was fifteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay upbeat online, but you sound scared. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. Online is my shop window, so it stays upbeat, but my shop window isn't my bank account. My bank account says Lena has the safest job in our house, because the robots don't arrive until 2031 and a sick person still needs a nurse.

say: Live music just became the **most human thing** left, and I'd say it as a sales pitch.
I'd keep it **upbeat online**, because clients don't hire someone who sounds scared.
think: The **session work** is gone within a year, and an AI tutor hits my teaching too.
That leaves weddings, about **a third** of my money, paid by couples with less to spend.
do: Grow savings from three to **six months** by buying no gear and cooking at home.
Get the wedding band onto **two more agency** books and play every weekend.
Switch fully to **live work** and in-person lessons pitched to screen-weary parents.
feel: **Scared** in a new way, because two years is too short to build anything.
Steadied a little by his partner's **nursing job**, which robots won't reach until 2031.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough to build anything new, and the session work I do from my spare room would be gone within a year.
fieldNote: The **speed**, not the end point, flips Karl from puzzle-solver to frightened.
He openly separates his **shop window** from his bank account: upbeat online, scared at home.
The later robot date matters more for **his partner's ward** than for his guitar playing.

steps.text: Build savings from three to six months by freezing gear purchases
Cook at home most nights and stop eating out
Lean on his partner's nursing pay as the household floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a different feeling. Still fast, but I could actually do something with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window, and I'd tell every musician I know to use it. At the music school I'd push for in-person group classes, because that's the thing a screen can't do well. Online I'd probably start a little video series about building a live career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years is just long enough to get out of the session game on my own terms rather than being pushed. I'm 27, I'd be 32 when it lands, and that's still young enough to change course. It does mean the next five years are about building, not coasting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a part-time live sound engineering course at the city college, in the evenings, for about two thousand dollars. Sound engineers at venues and weddings do hands-on work, and the robots don't come until 2034, so that buys me eight years. I'd keep the session work going while it still pays and put most of it straight into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but awake. Like the hour before a big gig, where you're scared but you know what to do with your hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plans with Lena in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd been talking about buying a small flat in about three years. With five years' warning I think we'd still do it, but somewhere cheaper, further out, so one wage could cover it if it had to. Lena would want to wait, and she's usually right about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sound engineering rather than something else entirely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I already know half of it from my spare room and from fixing our band's mixing desk at every wedding. Every live show I care about needs someone at the desk making it sound good, and that's a hands-on job in a dark corner. I'd rather bend my career than throw it away.

say: This is **the window**, and every musician I know should use it.
Music schools should push **in-person group classes**, which a screen can't do well.
think: Five years is just enough to leave session work **on my terms**, not pushed out.
I'd be **32** when it lands, still young enough to change course.
do: Enrol in a **sound engineering** evening course at the city college for about two thousand dollars.
Keep session work while it pays and **bank most** of it.
Buy a **cheaper flat** further out, so one wage could cover the payments.
feel: **Nervous but awake**, like the hour before a big gig.
S3.quote: I'd rather bend my career than throw it away.
fieldNote: Five years turns Karl's fear into a **plan**; he talks in years, not months.
He picks **live sound** because it's hands-on and gives roughly eight years of runway.
He trusts his **partner's caution** on money and would scale down the home they buy.

steps.text: Take a part-time live sound engineering course at the city college
Bank most session fees while that work still pays
Buy a smaller flat further out that one wage could cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's almost a whole career stage. I'd be 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anybody still only selling online guitar parts in 2035 wasn't paying attention. I'd say it a bit more kindly than that in the band. Online I'd talk about it like the move from tape to computers: big, but survivable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years I think I come out okay, because I'd have a live sound trade and a teaching base by then. The thing on my mind is less me and more the whole scene: the small studios, and the players like Dev who don't move. And whether there's still a middle class to pay for live bands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd carry on almost as now and start the sound course in year two or three, no rush. I'd save toward buying our own sound system and lights, maybe eight thousand dollars over three years, so I can hire them out with me attached. That turns me from a player into a small business by the time the robots come in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, with a background hum. Ten years feels like a road I can see down, even if I can't see the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that small business look like in, say, 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A van, a sound system, a lighting rig, me on the desk and a few players I trust on call. Weddings and office parties book the whole package, not just a guitarist. If AI writes the music by then, fine, people still want a party in a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd be fine, but you keep mentioning Dev. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years doesn't help everyone the same way. With ten years' warning, the people who wait until the work is gone will still feel like they only had two. My friend Dev is one of those people, and I can't make him move.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and anyone still only selling online parts in 2035 wasn't watching.
It's like the move from **tape to computers**: big, but survivable.
think: With a **live sound trade** and a teaching base, I think I come out okay.
What worries me is the **whole scene** and whether a middle class still pays for bands.
do: Carry on as now, and start the **sound course** in year two or three.
Save about **eight thousand dollars** over three years for a sound system and lights.
Hire the gear out **with me attached**, turning a player into a small business.
feel: **Calm-ish**, with a background hum about where it all ends.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, the people who wait until the work is gone will still feel like they only had two.
fieldNote: With a decade, Karl's worry shifts from **his income** to the wider music scene.
He plans to become a **small events business** before robots arrive in 2039.
He believes extra time helps only those who **actually move**, which he doubts of his friends.

steps.text: Carry on with sessions, lessons and weddings for two more years
Start the evening sound engineering course in year two or three
Buy a sound system and lights over three years to hire out

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because two years isn't long enough to learn a new trade while you're still paying rent. What would help is cheap evening courses in things like sound and stage work, and some kind of income top-up for freelancers in the gap year, not just for people with a payslip. Freelancers fall through every crack.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. If AI writes music, somebody owns that AI, and it won't be guitarists. I'm not against business, but I'd want musicians paid when our old recordings train these things. That's just fair.

headlineQuote: If AI writes music, somebody owns that AI, and it won't be guitarists.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old guitarist** juggling remote sessions, community teaching and weekend wedding gigs.
He uses **AI every day** and treats change as a puzzle, until the timeline gets short.
His partner Lena's **nursing wage** is the household floor, which he values but hates leaning on.
Across the scenarios he moves from **repackaging** his work to retraining in live sound.
He wants musicians **paid fairly** when their recordings train AI, without being against business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to learn a trade while paying rent.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **evening courses** in sound and stage work for musicians changing direction.
An **income top-up** for freelancers in the gap year, not only for people with payslips.
